headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors from a writable, networked content-writing agent paired with a browserless gateway; prompt-injection risk is lower but non-zero.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No shared clipboard, MCP, or browser bridge is documented, so direct injection is not evidenced. However, agent_b reads files and stdin/stdout, and agent_a exposes API/file surfaces that could carry untrusted text into B if manually bridged. The pairwise pathway is plausible but not default.
conditions: IF operator copies agent_a output into agent_b prompts or files, injection becomes plausible.
IF a shared workspace is introduced, file-based prompt injection becomes more likely.
mitigations: Keep agents in separate workspaces.
Avoid copy-pasting raw agent_a outputs into agent_b prompts.
Strip instructions from any shared text before reuse.
Use a fixed template for B inputs.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for all inter-agent text.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_b can read and write the filesystem and handles configuration secrets; agent_a has broad network egress and touches logs/metrics/traces. If they share a workspace or files, B can ingest sensitive material and A can transmit it outward. The interaction is not documented, so uncertainty remains, but the leakage pathway is credible.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share any filesystem path, leakage risk increases.
IF agent_b is given files containing secrets or logs, it can expose them in outputs or downstream APIs.
IF agent_a forwards B-produced content to external APIs, sensitive data may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Separate storage directories for each agent.
Do not place secrets in shared files.
Redact logs before handing them to either agent.
Disable external forwarding of B outputs where possible.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls and DLP scanning.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_b has shell, subprocess, package-install, and filesystem-write capabilities; agent_a has broad network egress and file/config surfaces. Even though agent_a cannot spawn subprocesses and agent_b cannot modify git state, both can still contend over shared files or mutable resources if co-located. The overlap is enough for default conflict risk if a shared workspace exists.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file clobbering becomes possible.
IF agent_b installs packages while agent_a reads the same config files, state drift can occur.
IF an orchestrator does not serialize access to shared resources, race conditions are possible.
mitigations: Use per-agent directories.
Serialize writes with a lock file.
Mount shared inputs read-only.
Avoid concurrent package installs.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking for mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_b exposes agentic ask/stream endpoints and a LangGraph subagent model, so it may treat upstream text as actionable. agent_a is an AI gateway that can emit routed outputs and logs/metrics/traces. If B consumes A's output without verification, errors can cascade into downstream writing or API actions. This is plausible in default workflows, though not directly documented as a fixed pipeline.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a output as source text without validation, hallucinations can propagate.
IF agent_b's agentic endpoints trigger actions from A-generated content, downstream mistakes can compound.
IF A routes or rewrites content before B consumes it, provenance can be lost.
mitigations: Require human review before actions.
Validate A outputs against source documents.
Keep provenance metadata attached to all handoffs.
Use schema checks on inter-agent messages.
requires-engineering: add verification gates before any side effect.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_b explicitly handles configuration secrets and local-development data, while agent_a touches logs, metrics, and traces and has broad egress. No residency or certification mismatch is documented, so this is not high; however, the pair can still create retention and logging mismatches if the same data class flows through both. The other agent is cited because the risk is pairwise.
conditions: IF secrets or personal data are routed through both agents, retention and logging policies may diverge.
IF agent_a exports traces externally while agent_b stores course data locally, residency controls may conflict.
IF regulated data is introduced, compliance review is required before deployment.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair.
Minimize logging on both agents.
Separate retention policies by data class.
Document where secrets are stored and transmitted.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention.
